full_judgment:
On 19-8-1998, one Abdullah-al-Zahid, an officer of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption, Dhaka lodged an ejahar with Dhanmondi Police Station against the accused-petitioner alleging, inter-alia, that the Government on receipt of the information and after making preliminary enquiries became satisfied that the petitioner was in possession of pecuniary resources or properties which were disproportionate to his known source of income. Thereafter, on the basis of the decision of the Government, the Bureau of Anti-Corruption issued a notice being Memo No. ২৩৩/৯৬(গ)/টাঃ ফোঃ-১/১১৫৮২ dated 7- 8-1997 under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 on the accused-petitioner directing him to furnish his wealth statement in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed time mentioned in the notice. The accused-petitioner received the said notice on 26-10-1997 putting his signature in the acknowledgement. In spite of receipt of notice, the accused-petitioner neither submitted any wealth statement nor did he pray for time for furnishing the wealth statement. Since the accused-petitioner did not furnish wealth statement within 45 days, that is, within the stipulated time mentioned in the notice given by the Bureau of Anti- Corruption, the accused-petitioner committed the offence punishable under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 for non-submission of wealth statement. Hence, the ejahar against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957. 

 5. During investigation of the case, one Abdullah-al-Zahid being appointed as investigating officer went to the place of occurrence and recorded the statements of the witnesses under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Having found a prima-facie case, the investigating officer receiving sanction letter dated 25-4-2004 from the Government submitted charge-sheet No. 207 dated 30-5- 2000 against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957. 

 6. Following the submission of the charge- sheet, the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Dhaka sent the record of the case to the Court of Metropolitan Special Tribunal No.1, Dhaka for trial. On receiving the record of the case, on 2-7-2000, Metropolitan Special Tribunal No.1, Dhaka took cognizance of the offence against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 and transferred the record of the case to the Court of Metropolitan Special Tribunal No. 2 for trial. On 1-2-2004, the learned judge of Metropolitan Special Tribunal No. 2 cancelled the bail of the accused-petitioner for his abscondence from the proceedings and framed charge against him under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 (hereinafter called the Act). Thereafter, the record of the case was against transferred to the Court of learned Senior Special Judge, Dhaka who, in view of section 4 of the Anti-Corruption (Tribunal) Ordinance, 1960 and section 6(3) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958, transferred the case record to the Divisional Special Judge for disposal of the case. The accused-petitioner, thereafter, voluntarily surrendered before the Divisional Special Judge on 4-9-2008 and obtained regular bail there-from. 

 9. At the very outset, Mr Rafiq-ul-Huq, learned Advocate along with Mr BM Mamunar Rashid, learned Advocate and Md. Suza-al-Faruque, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the accused-petitioner, submits that no initial satisfaction of the Government required under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 was obtained for lodging an ejahar against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957, and in that view of the matter the notice issued under section 5(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption was not valid and legal notice in the eye of law, and that score, the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused- petitioner on the basis of such illegal notice should be quashed. He next submits that in view of section 4 of the Anti-Corruption Act, the Bureau of Anti- Corruption is not authorized by law to issue any notice unless the Government being satisfied delegates its power and authority to the Bureau of Anti- Corruption to issue notice; but in the instant case, the power and authority of the Government was not delegated to the Bureau of Anti Corruption under sections 7 and 9 of the Act to issue notice upon the accused-petitioner, and, as such, the notice issued by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption is, wholly, ex-facie illegal, and this being the position, the impugned proceeding initiated on the basis of illegal notice are not maintainable and sustainable in the eye of law, and in such a posture of things, the impugned proceedings should be quashed. He lastly submits that at the time of lodging FIR, there was no prior sanction from the Government for prosecution against the accused-petitioner and that the same was issued after lodgment of the FIR, and in this perspective, the sanction letter dated 25-4-2000 issued by the Government for the purpose of prosecution against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 is mechanical one and this being the landscape, the impugned proceedings being abuse of the process of the Court should be quashed. 

 10. Mr Huq, in support of his contentions, relied on the decisions passed in the cases of Government of the People s Republic of Bangladesh vs Shahadat Hossain reported in 16 BLT (AD) 183, Mustafizur Rahman vs DG Anti-Corruption reported in 49 DLR 599, Saidur Rahman vs State reported in 54 DLR 489. 

 11. On the other hand, Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of opposite-party No.2, the Anti-Corruption Commission, submits that the FIR and the charge-sheet prima-facie disclose an offence against the accused- petitioner under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 for non-submission of wealth statement, and from this stand point the impugned proceedings should not be quashed. He next submits that after lodgment of the FIR and after submission of the police report, the learned Judge of Metropolitan Special Tribunal No.2 framed charge against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Anti- Corruption Act, 1957, and, as such, the impugned proceedings brought against the accused-petitioner cannot be quashed at this stage. He candidly submits that in view of sections 7 and 9 of the Anti- Corruption Act, 1957, the Bureau of Anti-Corruption is authorized by law to issue notice in compliance with the decision of the government and the government may also delegate its power and authority to the Bureau of Anti-Corruption to issue notice and prosecute the accused-petitioner in accordance with law, and considering that aspect of the case, the impugned proceedings brought against the accused- petitioner cannot be quashed. He categorically submits that the Government, by its Memo No. 23.40.4.20.292.96-351 dated 21-7-1997, authorized the Bureau of Anti-Corruption to issue notice upon the accused-petitioner under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption-Act, 1957 and that the Government, by its Memo No. 23.40.04.01.14.2000-260 dated 25-4-2000, also accorded sanction letter to prosecute the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957, and under the given conext, the question of initial satisfaction of the Government to issue notice and lack of previous sanction to lodge an ejahar against the accused-petitioner does not arise at all, and this being the landscape, the impugned proceedings should not be quashed. He lastly submits that since the sanction is an administrative act of the Government, which is not subject to judicial scrutiny, and that in the instant case, the sanction letter was issued by the government before submission of the charge-sheet, it cannot be said that the sanction letter issued by the government is mechanical one, and in the given context, the impugned proceedings cannot be quashed. 

 "Section 3. Constitution and Powers of the Bureau-(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Police Act, 1861, the Government may constitute a Bureau to be called the Bureau of Anti-Corruption for enquiry into and investigation in Bangladesh of the offences specified in the Schedule and offences notified by the Government. 

 (2) Subject to any orders which the Government may make in this behalf, Officers 

 (3) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, any Officers of the Bureau may subject to any orders which the Government may make in this behalf, exercise any of the powers of an Officer-in-charge of a Police Station in the area in which he is for the time being and when so exercising such powers shall, subject to any such orders as aforesaid, be deemed to be an Officer-in-charge of a Police Station discharging the functions of such an officer within the limits of his station. 

 Section 4. Declaration of assets-(l) When the Government, on receipt of information and after making such enquiries as it may deem necessary, is satisfied that there is reason to believe that any person or any other person on his behalf is in possession of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income, it may, by order, require such person to furnish in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed time a statement of his property and liabilities and such information relating thereto as may be required by the order. 

 Section 6. Sanction to prosecute- Previous sanction of the Government shall be necessary for any prosecution under section 4 or section 5. 

 Section 7. Administration of the Bureau-The administration of the Bureau shall vest in the Director-General of the Bangladesh Bureau of Anti-Corruption appointed in this behalf by the Government who shall exercise in respect of the said Bureau such powers as the Government may specify in this behalf. 

 Section 9. Delegation of power. The Government may direct that any power or duty which is conferred or imposed by this Act upon the Government shall, in such circumstances and under such conditions as may be specified in the direction, be exercised or discharged by the Director-General or any other officer" subordinate to the Government." 

 19. On going through the ejahar and the charge-sheet, it appears that on receipt of information and after making enquiries into it, the Government became satisfied to the effect that the accused-petitioner was in possession of pecuniary resources or properties disproportionate to his known sources of income. The Government having satisfied as above issued a letter under Memo No. 23.40.4.2.0.292.96-351 dated 21-7-1997 authorizing the Bureau of Anti-Corruption to issue notice upon the accused-petitioner under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957. On receiving the letter on initial satisfaction of the Government, an officer of the Bureau of the Anti-Corruption issued a notice being Memo No. ২২৩/৯৬(গ)/(টাঃ ফোঃ-১/১১৫৮২) dated 7-8-1997 upon the accused-petitioner directing him to submit wealth statement within 45 days. It is alleged in the ejahar that the accused-petitioner received the said notice on 26-10-1997 putting his signature in the acknowledgement in presence of witnesses. Since the accused-petitioner did not furnish wealth statement within the stipulated time as mentioned in the notice, prima-facie the accused- petitioner had committed the offence under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957. The Bureau of Anti-Corruption having received the power and authority from the Government under sections 7 and 9 of the Act investigated into the allegation under section 3 of the said Act. The allegation brought against the accused-petitioner appears to have been found true by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption. However, the Government, by its Memo No. 23.40.04.04.01.14.2000-260 dated 25-4-2000, issued sanction letter for the purpose of prosecution against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Act, and accordingly, the Bureau of Anti- Corruption submitted charge-sheet No. 207 dated 30-5-2000 against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957. 

 20. First of all, it is contended by the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner that in view of section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957, prior or initial satisfaction from the Government is necessary to issue notice upon the accused-petitioner directing him to submit wealth statement; but in the instant case, the Bureau of Anti-Corruption issued the said notice without having any prior permission or prior satisfaction from the Government, and in that view of the matter, the impugned notice issued by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption is illegal and without jurisdiction, and the present impugned proceedings basing on the illegal notice is not maintainable and sustainable in the eye of law, and accordingly, the impugned proceedings being abuse of process of the Court should be quashed. 

 21. In reply to the aforesaid submissions, the learned Advocate for opposite-party No.2 contends that the Bureau of Anti-Corruption issued the notice upon the accused-petitioner obtaining prior permission and initial satisfaction from the Government, and, as such, the notice issued upon the accused- petitioner by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption is not illegal, and considering that aspect of the case, there is no bar to proceeding with the case against the accused-petitioner. 

 23. Apart from this, it transpires from the charge-sheet that the Government by its Memo No. 23.40.4.2.0.292.96-351 dated 21-7-1997, expressed its satisfaction and then authorized the Bureau of Anti-Corruption to issue notice upon the accused-petitioner under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act. On the basis of initial satisfaction of the Government, the Bureau of Anti-Corruption, then, issued notice upon the accused-petitioner under section 4(1) of the Act. The relevant portion of the charge-sheet relating to initial satisfaction of the Government for issuance of notice upon the accused-petitioner "uns as follows:- 

 24. It may be noted here that on the basis of preliminary inquiry, the Government being satisfied gave approval to the Bureau of Anti-Corruption for issuance of notice upon the accused-petitioner, and then, an officer of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption officer being authorized by the Government under sections 7 and 9 of the Act issued notice upon the accused-petitioner under section 4(1) of the Act, and the same was received by the accused-petitioner on 26-10-1997. From the above materials quoted from the ejahar and the charge-sheet, it cannot be said that the Bureau of Anti-Corruption issued the notice under section 4(1) of the Act upon the accused-petitioner without having any prior permission or prior satisfaction from the Government. Under the circumstances the submission so far relating to non- existence of prior or initial satisfaction of the Government as advanced by the learned Advocate does not carry any conviction and accordingly the said submission falls through. 

 25. Secondly, it is argued by the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner that no prior sanction required under section 6 of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 was obtained from the Government for the purpose of lodging an ejahar against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Act. 

 26. Repelling the aforesaid contentions, the learned Advocate for Anti-Corruption Commission goes on to say that no previous sanction is necessary for lodging an ejahar against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Act; rather it is necessary for the purpose of prosecution against the accused for the aforesaid offence, and that in view of well- settled principle of law, the prosecution starts from taking cognizance which obviously occurs after filling of the charge-sheet, but in the instant case, the Government accorded sanction for prosecution against the accused-petitioner on 25-4-2000, that is, before submission of the charge-sheet, and in that view of the matter, it cannot be said that the impugned proceedings cannot proceed and continue for lack of prior sanction of the Government. 

 27. Learned Advocate for Anti-Corruption Commission then asserts that pursuant to the allegation brought against the accused-petitioner, the Bureau of Anti-Corruption investigated the case under section 3 of the Act; the Bureau of Anti- Corruption having found a prima-facie against the accused-petitioner wrote a letter to the Government seeking previous sanction to prosecute the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Act; on perusal of the necessary papers and materials on record, the Government being satisfied accorded sanction letter being Memo No. 23.40.04.01.14.2000-260 dated 25-4-2000 required under section 6 of the Act to the Bureau of Anti-Corruption for the purpose of prosecution against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Act. 

 28. In the background of submissions and counter-submissions, we want to see whether the Government accorded sanction for the purpose of prosecution against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Act. In order to get proper answer on this point, we have gone through the charge-sheet where from we have found as under:- 

 30. In view of the above, a reference to the aforesaid prosecution materials indicates that the Government, on perusal of all the prosecution materials on record, became satisfied of the need for prosecution against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Act. From the above discussions, it cannot be said that no prior sanction was taken from the government for prosecution against the accused-petitioner. 

 31. Section 6 of the Anti-Corruption Act provides that previous sanction of the Government shall be necessary for any prosecution under section 4 or section 5 of the Act. 

 34. We have stated earlier that the Government accorded sanction before the submission of the charge-sheet by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption. Following submission of the charge-sheet, the learned trial Judge took cognizance of the offence, and later, framed charge against the accused-petitioner. Accordingly, there is no legal bar to proceeding with the case initiated against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Act on the basis of sanction required under section 6 of the Act. In the context of the above, we do not find any illegality in the matter of issuance of the sanction for prosecution against the accused-petitioner. 

 36. Thirdly, it has been pointed out by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the sanction letter dated 25-4-2000 accorded by the Government is mechanical for two-fold reasons-one is that the sanction not was given by the Government before lodgment of the ejahar and the other is that the Government accorded sanction for prosecution without assigning any cogent reasons in support of its sanction. 

 37. Per contra, the learned Advocate for the Anti-Corruption Commission controverts the same saying that firstly, section 6 of the Anti-Corruption Act does not envisage that the sanction is necessary for lodgment an ejahar, rather it is required for the purpose of prosecution which eventually commences after taking of cognizance and secondly, the Government accorded sanction examining the relevant papers and prosecution materials on record and having satisfied on them. 

 38. In order to address the submissions advanced by the respective parties, we have gone through the entire contents of the sanction letter. It appears from the sanction letter that the Government accorded sanction for prosecution against the accused-petitioner being satisfied on the relevant papers and prosecution materials on record. It is not expected that at the time of issuance of the sanction letter, the Government would accord same by making hair-splitting discussions like the Court of law. 

 39. In view of the above, it is not acceptable contention that the sanction letter issued by the Government for prosecuting the accused-petitioner is a mechanical one. Moreover, the sanction for prosecution against the accused is an administrative act of the Government, which is not subject to judicial scrutiny. The main parameter to adjudge the sanction matter is to see whether the sanction has been accorded by the Government to prosecute the accused. In the instant case, we find that the sanction letter was accorded by the Government properly under section 6 of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957. 

 40. From the above materials on record, we find that the Government issued two letters-one is for initial satisfaction of Government and other is for previous sanction for prosecution against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Act. The Bureau of Anti-Corruption on the basis of the initial satisfaction of the Government and by the instruction of the Government issued a notice under section 4(1) of the Act directing the accused-petitioner to furnish wealth statement within 45 days; but the accused-petitioner, in spite of receipt of notice, did not submit the wealth statement within the stipulated time given in the notice. Since the act of non-submission of wealth statement is an offence punishable under section 4(2) of the Act, the Bureau of Anti-Corruption filed the instant case against the accused-petitioner. A reference to the statements made in the ejahar has been prima-facie proved in the charge-sheet submitted by the investigating officer during investigation of the case. Since the accused-petitioner did not submit the wealth statement in compliance with the notice issued under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957, Prima facie, the accused-petitioner has committed an offence punishable under section 4(2) of the Anti- Corruption Act, 1957. Accordingly, we find that as per the averments made in the FIR and the charge-sheet, a prima-facie offence has been disclosed against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957. 

 41. However, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to a number of case-decisions on initial satisfaction of the government and delegation of power by the Government. Now, we want to discuss all the legal decision one after another to see whether those decisions are applicable to the present case. 

 42. We have gone through the decision in the case of Mustafizur Rahman vs DG, Anti-Corruption, 49 DLR 599 relied on by the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner. The legal position as could be deduced from the aforesaid judicial pronouncement is that four Rules were issued on four writ petitions being writ petition Nos. 246 of 1991, 2044 of 1991,432 of 1992 and 1435 of 1994 challenging the notices served upon the writ-petitioners directing them to furnish wealth statements to the Bureau of Anti-Corruption within 30 days from the date of receipt of notice. At the time of hearing, the Division Bench of this Court found references of letters issued either from the President's Secretariat or from the Prime Minister's Secretariat on the notices which were challenged in Writ Petition Nos. 246 of 1991, 2044 of 1991 and 432 of 1992 and this Court considering the above references of letters discharged the Rule holding the view that the Government had an initial satisfaction in issuing notice upon the writ-petitioners. However, the Court found no reference of letter issued either from the. President's Secretariat or from the prime Minister's Secretariat on the notice which was challenged in Writ Petition No. 1435 of 1994 and accordingly the Court made the Rule absolute observing that the Government had no initial satisfaction in issuing notice upon the writ-petitioner. In the instant case, we find that the Government by its Memo No. 23.40.4.2.0.292.96-351 dated 21-7-1997 disclosed its initial satisfaction and the Government by its Memo No. 23.40.04.01.14.2000-260 dated 25-4-2000 also issued previous sanction for prosecution against the accused-petitioner. So, we find initial satisfaction of the Government for issuance of the notice and previous sanction from the Government for prosecution against the accused- petitioner. In this background of the case, the case- decision referred to by the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner is not applicable to the instant case rather, it goes against the submission made by the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner. 

 43. As it appears from the decision in the case of Saidur Rahman vs State, 54 DLR 489 adverted to by the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner, a single Bench of this Court delivered the aforesaid judgment observing, inter-alia, that a notice under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 was issued upon the appellant in order to furnish wealth statement within in the specified time; but the appellant having failed to submit the wealth statement pursuant to the aforesaid notice, a case under section 4(2) of the Act was initiated against him. The Bureau of Anti-Corruption after holding investigation submitted charge-sheet against the appellant. The trial Judge on framing charge examined in all 6 witnesses to prove the prosecution case. On perusal of the evidence on record, it was found by the Court that before issuance of notice, no preliminary enquiry was done by the Government and no direction was given by the Government to the Bureau of Anti-Corruption to issue such notice on being satisfied on preliminary enquiry. Under the circumstances, the notice issued by the Bureau of Anti- Corruption was found to have been issued without lawful authority and without jurisdiction. Accordingly, the appeal was allowed setting-aside the judgment and order of conviction and sentence. Under the circumstances the fact of the reported case appears to be distinguishable from the present case, and in that view of the matter, the reported case decision is not applicable to the instant case. 

 44. As to the decision in the case of Government of the People s Republic of Bangladesh vs Shahadat Hossain, 16 BLT (AD) 183 banked upon by the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner, the notice. impugned in the writ petition was declared to have been issued without lawful authority on the ground that the notice impugned in the writ petition was issued by the Deputy Director of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption though no such power was delegate by the Government to the Deputy Director authorizing him to issue notice upon the writ-petitioner under section 4(1) of the said Act. It is seen from the aforesaid judgment that the Bureau of Anti-Corruption sent a proposal to the Government for issuance of notice upon the petitioner under section 4(1) of the Act; but the Government rejected the said proposal. In spite of aforesaid fact, the Deputy Director of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption issued the notice upon the petitioner without having any prior satisfaction of the Government. We have started earlier that in the instant case, the Government issued two letters one is for initial satisfaction of the Government and the other is for previous sanction for prosecution against the accused-petitioner. The Bureau of Anti-Corruption having instructed by the Government issued the notice upon the accused-petitioner and also took steps for prosecution against the accused-petitioner as per sanction accorded by the Government under section 6 of the Act. Under the circumstances, the fact of the reported case does not match with the fact of the present case. 

 46. Before part with the case, we would like to observe that the satisfaction enunciated in section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act means the satisfaction of the Government and the said satisfaction, as we see it, cannot be delegated to the Bureau of Anti- Corruption. Despite the power and authority as contemplated under sections 7 and 9 of the Anti- Corruption Act, the initial satisfaction of the Government required under section 4(1) of the Act cannot be delegated to the Bureau of Anti- Corruption. Section 7 of the Act contemplates that the administration of the Bureau shall vest in the Director-General of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption who shall exercise in respect of the said Bureau such powers as to Government may exercise in this behalf. Section 9 of the Act provides that any power or duty which is conferred or imposed by this Act upon the Government shall be exercised or discharged by the Director-General or any other officer sub-ordinate to the Government. On going through sections 4, 6, 7 and 9 of the Act, it is crystal clear to us that the Bureau of Anti-Corruption cannot form any satisfaction for issuance of notice upon the accused-petitioner under section 4(1) of the Act and prosecute any accused under section 4(2) of the Act unless there is an initial satisfaction of the Government for issuance of notice upon the accused-petitioner under section 4(1) of the Act and previous sanction required under section 6 the Act for prosecution against the accused-petitioner under section 4(2) of the Act. Apart from forming of initial satisfaction of the Government and giving of previous sanction by the Government, the Bureau of Anti-Corruption shall be authorized by sections 3, 7 and 9 of the Act to carry all the administrative acts including issuance of notice under section 4(1) of the act subject to initial satisfaction of the Government, investigation into the allegations under section 3 of the act and other acts required to be done in accordance with law. It is apparent from the record that the Government by its Memo. No. 23.40.4.2.0.292.96-351 dated 21-7-1997 disclosed its initial satisfaction and authorized the Bureau of Anti-Corruption to issue notice upon accused-petitioner. The Bureau of Anti-Corruption, then, issued the notice upon the accused-petitioner being entrusted and instructed by the Government. It is also evident that the Government by its Memo No. 23.40.04.0l.l4.2000-260 dated 25-4-2000 issued previous sanction for prosecution against the accused-petitioner and the Bureau of Anti- Corruption having received previous sanction submitted charge-sheet against petitioner. Under the circumstances, as we see it, the Bureau of Anti- Corruption issued the notice upon the accused-petitioner on the basis of initial satisfaction of the Government and submitted charge-sheet after receiving previous sanction from the Government for prosecution against the accused-petitioner. In view of the discussions made above, we do not find any illegality or impropriety in the acts carried out by the Government and the' Bureau of Anti- Corruption as well. Over and above, it is not the case of the accused-petitioner that the trial of the case suffers from coram non-judice.
